entries.meaning: The immature form of an insect or other animal.
examples: The larva burrows into the wood.
Mosquito larvae live in standing water.
Thousands of larvae hatched overnight.
A single larva can destroy an entire leaf.
The larvae were collected for the study.

senses.head: The immature stage
examples: The larva burrows into the wood.
Mosquito larvae live in standing water.
Thousands of larvae hatched overnight.
A single larva can destroy an entire leaf.
The larvae were collected for the study.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the larvae hatch in spring
entries.variants: ✗ larvas is not used in scientific or general writing
entries.contrast: This is one of the -ae plurals with no regular competitor at all. The adjective is larval.

entries.meaning: One of the bones of the spine.
examples: He cracked a vertebra in the accident.
The human spine has thirty-three vertebrae.
Two vertebrae had fused together.
The lowest vertebra takes the most load.
X-rays showed damage to several vertebrae.

senses.head: A spinal bone
examples: He cracked a vertebra in the accident.
The human spine has thirty-three vertebrae.
Two vertebrae had fused together.
The lowest vertebra takes the most load.
X-rays showed damage to several vertebrae.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the vertebrae are fused
entries.variants: both /-breɪ/ and /-briː/ are accepted in American English
entries.contrast: ✗ A vertebrae for one bone is a very common error — the singular is vertebra, without the e. The adjective is vertebral, and vertebrate is a separate noun meaning an animal with a backbone.

entries.meaning: Simple photosynthetic organisms living mainly in water.
examples: Green algae covered the surface of the pond.
A single alga is invisible without a microscope.
Algae bloom when the water warms.
The tank needs cleaning — the algae are back.
Some algae produce toxins dangerous to dogs.

senses.head: The organisms
examples: Green algae covered the surface of the pond.
A single alga is invisible without a microscope.
Algae bloom when the water warms.
The tank needs cleaning — the algae are back.
Some algae produce toxins dangerous to dogs.

entries.countability: countable, and usually used as a plural mass noun
entries.agreement: plural verb — algae are blooming in the lake
entries.contrast: The singular alga is almost never used — in practice the word is algae, and the g changes sound between them: /ɡ/ in AL-guh, /dʒ/ in AL-jee. Most speakers treat algae as a mass noun taking a singular verb in casual speech: algae is covering the pond.

entries.meaning: A rule expressed in symbols; a fixed method; also infant milk.
examples: Apply the quadratic formula.
Both formulas give the same answer.
The book lists all the relevant formulae.
There is no formula for a good marriage.
The studio keeps reusing the same formula.
The baby takes formula at night.

senses.head: A mathematical or chemical rule
examples: Apply the quadratic formula.
Both formulas give the same answer.
The book lists all the relevant formulae.

senses.head: A fixed method or recipe for success
examples: There is no formula for a good marriage.
The studio keeps reusing the same formula.

senses.head: Infant milk
examples: The baby takes formula at night.

entries.countability: countable, and uncountable in the baby-food sense
entries.agreement: plural verb — the formulas are equivalent
entries.variants: formulas dominates American English; formulae survives in mathematical writing
entries.contrast: Both are correct, but formulas is now the default even in most technical prose. In American English formula also means infant milk, and in that sense it is uncountable: we're out of formula.

entries.meaning: A metal device for sending or receiving signals; also a sensory feeler on an insect.
examples: The antenna on the roof came down in the storm.
Both antennas need to point the same way.
Cell antennas are hidden inside the steeple.
The beetle waved its antennae.
A moth's antennae detect scent from miles away.
Her political antennae are extremely good.

senses.head: A radio or television aerial
examples: The antenna on the roof came down in the storm.
Both antennas need to point the same way.
Cell antennas are hidden inside the steeple.

senses.head: An insect's feeler
examples: The beetle waved its antennae.
A moth's antennae detect scent from miles away.

senses.head: Figuratively — sensitivity to something
examples: Her political antennae are extremely good.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the antennas were replaced
entries.contrast: The plural depends on the meaning, and this split is consistent. Metal on a roof: antennas. Feelers on a bug: antennae. The figurative sense — sensitivity to something — takes antennae.

entries.meaning: A cloud of gas and dust in space.
examples: The Orion Nebula is visible with binoculars.
Several nebulae appear in the same field of view.
A nebula is where new stars form.
These nebulae glow in ultraviolet light.
The telescope photographed a planetary nebula.

senses.head: The astronomical object
examples: The Orion Nebula is visible with binoculars.
Several nebulae appear in the same field of view.
A nebula is where new stars form.
These nebulae glow in ultraviolet light.
The telescope photographed a planetary nebula.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the nebulae are visible in infrared
entries.variants: nebulae is preferred in astronomy; nebulas is accepted
entries.contrast: The related adjective nebulous means vague — a figurative extension of 'cloudy'.

entries.meaning: The single-celled organism that moves by changing shape.
examples: An amoeba has no fixed shape.
The slide showed dozens of amoebas.
Amoebae reproduce by simple division.
A rare amoeba caused the infection.
The committee is an amoeba — it changes shape every month.

senses.head: The organism
examples: An amoeba has no fixed shape.
The slide showed dozens of amoebas.
Amoebae reproduce by simple division.
A rare amoeba caused the infection.

senses.head: Figuratively — something shapeless
examples: The committee is an amoeba — it changes shape every month.

entries.variants: amoebas is commoner in American English; the British spelling is amoeba or amœba
entries.contrast: Both plurals are correct. The adjective amoebic appears in amoebic dysentery.

entries.meaning: A woman who is a former student of a school or college.
examples: She is an alumna of the same college.
The alumnae organized the reunion.
Three alumnae sit on the board.
As an alumna, she gets the newsletter.
Both alumnae spoke at the ceremony.

senses.head: A female graduate
examples: She is an alumna of the same college.
The alumnae organized the reunion.
Three alumnae sit on the board.
As an alumna, she gets the newsletter.
Both alumnae spoke at the ceremony.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the alumnae established the fund
entries.variants: the informal sex-neutral alum / alums is now very common in American usage
entries.contrast: Four forms to keep straight, and the two plurals differ by a single sound: alumni /-naɪ/ for men or a mixed group, alumnae /-niː/ for women only. Mixed groups always take alumni.
